statement: Flags are put along a path 12 m long. There is a flag at each end and a flag every 3 m. How many flags are there?

choices.misconception: I worked out 12 shared into 3 m gaps, which counts the gaps, not the flags.
I counted the 4 gaps and then added a flag for each end on top.
I gave the length of the path in metres instead of the number of flags.
I added 12 and 3 instead of seeing how many 3 m gaps fit.

hints: Draw the path and put the first flag at the start.
A small drawing shows that flags and gaps are not the same count. Mark a flag, then a 3 m gap, then a flag, and keep going until you reach the far end.
Flags stand at 0, 3, 6 and so on, up to 12 m. List those places and count them.

solutions.reliable: Flags stand at 0 m, 3 m, 6 m, 9 m and 12 m. That is 5 flags. There are only 4 gaps between them. The idea to keep: in a row with something at both ends, there is always one more post than gap.
solutions.elegant: 12 m shared into 3 m gaps gives 4 gaps. A row with flags at both ends has one more flag than gaps, so 4 + 1 = 5. The idea to keep: count the gaps, then add one.

whyOnTest: Drawing the situation is the quickest way to catch a gaps-versus-flags mistake, and two choices come from it.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
